intro.title: Discover Tritons’ Fountain
intro.description: Tritons’ Fountain is one of Malta's most famous landmarks, located in the square outside the City Gate of Valletta, in Floriana. This magnificent bronze fountain, built in 1959 and designed by sculptor Vincent Apap, features three mythological Tritons holding up a massive basin, symbolizing Malta's deep connection with the sea.

visitGuide.title: Visit Tips
items: The fountain square is spacious and flat, perfect for a leisurely walk and taking photos.
The fountain is beautifully illuminated at night, making it an excellent spot for night views and romantic strolls.
The square is highly accessible and serves as the main gateway to the historic city of Valletta.

sections.title: Historical Background
sections.content: Tritons’ Fountain was constructed in 1959, designed by renowned Maltese sculptor Vincent Apap and draughtsman Victor Anastasi. It was built to decorate the newly constructed bus terminus and quickly became a symbol of Malta's independence and national identity.

sections.title: Design & Architecture
sections.content: The main structure of the fountain consists of three bronze Triton figures jointly holding up a massive basin. Water overflows from the basin, creating beautiful cascades. The base is constructed from limestone, echoing the historical architectural style of the surroundings.

sections.title: Cultural Significance
sections.content: As a landmark outside Valletta's City Gate, Tritons’ Fountain is not only a popular photo spot for tourists but also a central square for local residents to gather, celebrate festivals, and host major public events.

sections.title: Restoration & Preservation
sections.content: The fountain underwent a comprehensive restoration between 2017 and 2018, removing years of grime and damage to restore the bronze statues to their original glory. The square was also redesigned to become a fully pedestrianized public space.

officialManagement.title: About Tritons’ Fountain
officialManagement.text: Tritons’ Fountain is a significant landmark and public monument in Malta. The structure is routinely maintained and managed by relevant municipal departments and heritage authorities to ensure its pristine condition as a national symbol.

entity.aboutText: Welcome to Tritons’ Fountain, widely recognized as the central Tritons Fountain. Located in the heart of Floriana, Malta, this landmark is the main gateway for travelers entering the historic capital of Valletta.
entity.locationHeading: Location & How to Visit Tritons Fountain in Floriana
entity.locationText: Tritons’ Fountain stands in an open public square just outside the City Gate of Valletta, in Floriana (Il-Furjana), Malta. The square is spacious, flat, and free to visit around the clock, making it an easy first stop on any trip to the capital.
entity.landmarksText: When visiting Tritons’ Fountain, visitors can easily explore surrounding historical landmarks and points of interest, including the Valletta City Gate and St. John’s Co-Cathedral.
entity.historyText: Designed by Maltese sculptor Vincent Apap and completed in 1959, Tritons’ Fountain quickly became a symbol of Malta’s independence and national identity, and today anchors the entrance to Valletta’s UNESCO-listed old town.

items.question: Where is Tritons’ Fountain located?
items.answer: Tritons’ Fountain is located in Floriana (Il-Furjana), Malta, immediately outside the City Gate of Valletta.

items.question: Is Tritons Fountain free to visit?
items.answer: Yes, Tritons’ Fountain is a public monument and is free to visit year-round, open 24 hours a day.

items.question: What are the opening hours of Tritons’ Fountain?
items.answer: The fountain stands in an open public square and is accessible 24 hours a day, every day of the year.

items.question: How do I get to Tritons’ Fountain?
items.answer: It is about a 1-minute walk from the Valletta City Gate and sits right next to the Valletta bus terminus; direct airport buses also stop nearby.

items.question: Who designed Tritons’ Fountain?
items.answer: It was designed by the Maltese sculptor Vincent Apap together with draughtsman Victor Anastasi, and was completed in 1959.

items.question: What is there to see near Tritons’ Fountain?
items.answer: Right beside it is the Valletta City Gate, and within a short walk are St. John’s Co-Cathedral, the Upper Barrakka Gardens, and Republic Square in Valletta.

items.question: Are there beaches near Tritons’ Fountain and Valletta?
items.answer: Valletta is a fortified city with a rocky coastline rather than sandy beaches. For swimming, the closest spots are the Sliema waterfront and Exiles Bay (a short ferry or walk across the harbour), with larger sandy beaches such as St. Julian’s, Mellieħa and Golden Bay a bus ride away.

items.question: When is the best time to visit and photograph Tritons’ Fountain?
items.answer: The square faces open sky, so golden hour and blue hour give the warmest light on the bronze Tritons, while after sunset the fountain is illuminated and reflective — ideal for night photography. Mornings are the quietest.

responsibility.title: Visitor Responsibility & Heritage Care
responsibility.subtitle: A few simple habits keep this shared public space enjoyable for everyone.

items.name: Respect the Monument
items.desc: The Tritons and basin are protected heritage. Please do not climb, sit on, or enter the water — it is decorative, not for swimming or drinking.

items.name: Zero Litter
items.desc: Use the public bins around the square. During festivals the area gets busy, so take your rubbish with you if bins are full.

items.name: Urban Wildlife
items.desc: Pigeons and gulls gather here. Enjoy them from a distance and avoid feeding them, which harms their health and the square.

items.name: Water & Sun Safety
items.desc: Malta's sun is strong in summer. Carry water, use sunscreen, and take shade breaks — the square has limited natural shade.

items.name: Events & Crowds
items.desc: The square hosts national celebrations. Check local listings and expect larger crowds on public holidays.

transportGuide.title: Getting to Tritons' Fountain — Step by Step
transportGuide.subtitle: The fountain sits right at the Valletta bus terminus, just outside the City Gate.

airport.name: From Malta International Airport (MLA)
steps: Take the direct airport bus (route X4) to the Valletta terminus — about 40 minutes.
Taxis and ride-hailing apps cover the same trip in roughly 20–25 minutes.
From the terminus, the fountain is a 1-minute walk through the main square.

public.name: By Public Bus
steps: Almost every route on Malta terminates at the Valletta bus terminus.
Buy a tallinja card or use contactless payment before boarding.
The fountain is the first thing you see as you step into the square.

taxi.name: By Taxi / Ride-Hailing
steps: Licensed white taxis and app-based services can drop you at the City Gate.
Ask the driver for 'Valletta City Gate' or 'Tritons Fountain'.
There is a designated set-down point at the edge of the square.

parking.name: By Car & Parking
steps: Driving into Valletta is restricted; park at a public car park outside the walls (MCP / Mateo Falcón).
From the car park it is a short walk to the square.
Avoid on-street parking in Floriana during peak hours.

stories.title: Stories, Symbolism & Heritage
stories.subtitle: Beyond the bronze and water, the fountain carries decades of Maltese memory.

items.title: The Tritons of Myth
items.content: In Greek myth, Tritons were messenger-gods of the sea with the body of a fish and the torso of a man. Sculptor Vincent Apap reimagined three of them heaving up a great shell-shaped basin — a nod to Malta's enduring bond with the Mediterranean.

items.title: A Symbol of Independence
items.content: Unveiled in 1959, the fountain rose as Malta moved toward self-government and, later, full independence in 1964. For many Maltese it became an emblem of national identity.

items.title: Guardian of the City Gate
items.content: For generations the fountain has been the threshold between the modern city and the fortified old town of Valletta, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980.

items.title: The 2017–2018 Restoration
items.content: A full restoration stripped decades of grime, repaired the bronze, and returned the square to pedestrians — a transformation locals still talk about.
